candidateRows: The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent, personal cause beyond space and time.
This is the opening cosmological case and supplies Craig's principal route from the universe's beginning to a personal creator.
Craig combines philosophical objections to an actually infinite past with cosmological evidence, then infers an immaterial and personal cause.
The life-permitting fine-tuning of the universe is best explained by intelligent design rather than necessity or chance.
Fine-tuning is one of Craig's five expressly enumerated reasons for theism and directly supports a cosmic designer.
Craig describes narrowly life-permitting constants and initial conditions, excludes physical necessity and chance, and concludes design.
Objective moral values and duties exist, and their existence requires God as their adequate foundation.
The argument is Craig's principal moral case for God and is intended to establish the creator's moral character.
Craig argues that naturalism cannot make morality objectively binding, while moral experience warrants belief in real values and duties.
The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' belief are best explained by Jesus' resurrection, which entails God's existence.
This is the specifically Christian historical argument connecting alleged facts about Jesus directly to the existence of God.
Craig identifies three claimed historical facts, rejects familiar naturalistic accounts, and infers that Jesus rose from the dead.
A person can know that God exists directly through personal experience, independently of propositional arguments.
The claim supplies Craig's independent experiential basis for theism even if the preceding public arguments remain disputed.
Craig presents awareness of God as an immediate experienced reality and maintains that sincere seekers can encounter that reality personally.
The debate concerns a highly specific Christian-God hypothesis that bears the burden of evidential support among many supernatural alternatives.
This framing defines the proposition Millican contests and establishes the burden structure governing his entire skeptical case.
Craig's conclusion that atheism needs its own proof and must defeat all five theistic arguments.
Millican defines the disputed claim as traditional Christian theism and emphasizes that it is one specific factual hypothesis among many.
Human tendencies and cultural transmission generate conflicting religions, so common religious belief-forming methods are unreliable guides to truth.
The argument undermines religious testimony, upbringing, authority, texts, and experience as dependable support for the Christian hypothesis.
Millican links religious belief to agency detection, social power, geography, and inherited culture, then argues that incompatible outputs defeat reliability.
Given numerous rival religions and no solid evidence for disembodied minds, Christian theism requires an exceptionally strong case and should otherwise be rejected.
This passage supplies Millican's central standard for deciding the motion and his explicit route from insufficient evidence to atheism.
Craig's claim that theism is rational unless Millican both defeats five arguments and independently proves atheism.
Millican rejects equal prior probabilities, cites dependence of thought on brains, and argues that Christianity competes with thousands of alternatives.
Experience of ordinary causal change does not justify the claim that anything beginning from nothing must have a cause.
The move attacks a necessary premise of Craig's cosmological argument by disputing its experiential and empirical justification.
Craig's cosmological premise that whatever begins to exist must have a transcendent cause.
Millican distinguishes rearrangements of existing matter from creation from nothing and invokes apparently random quantum events against the inference.
Observed causes are physical, but the total physical universe cannot have that kind of cause, and causation outside time is difficult to understand.
The argument challenges applying familiar causal principles to the universe as a whole and contests the coherence of a timeless creator.
Craig's inference from caused beginnings within reality to a timeless cause of the entire physical universe.
Millican argues that extrapolation from physical parts to the whole risks composition error and that known causes operate temporally.
Neither the local universe's beginning nor the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem establishes that the global physical universe had an absolute beginning.
This challenges the second premise of Craig's cosmological argument and disputes the inference from current cosmology to an absolute beginning.
Craig's claim that cosmological evidence and the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem show that the universe began to exist.
After challenging causal principles, Millican distinguishes local from global universes, identifies possible past-eternal models, and emphasizes the limits of present physics.
Even if the physical universe had a nonphysical cause, identifying that cause as an immaterial mind exceeds the evidence and our cognitive competence.
The move attacks the cosmological argument's crucial transition from an unexplained or nonphysical cause to a personal theistic creator.
Craig's inference that any cause of the physical universe must be a timeless, immaterial, personal mind.
Millican argues that disembodied minds lack evidential support and that any nonphysical cosmic cause could belong to a category beyond evolved human understanding.
Craig must define objective moral values precisely and show both that they exist in that sense and that their existence requires God.
This contests both the conceptual premise and the evidential premise of the moral argument rather than merely proposing an alternative moral theory.
Craig's argument that objective moral values and duties exist only if God exists and therefore support theism.
Millican notes that several atheistic ethical theories treat moral standards as independent of popular belief, then demands a God-dependent definition and supporting evidence.
Millican has not supplied a comparably good argument for atheism, because denying God requires justification and religious diversity does not undermine Craig's evidential method.
The move defends Craig's second overarching debate contention and addresses the burden of proof and reliability framework governing the whole exchange.
Millican's burden-of-proof argument and his claim that culturally diverse religious belief undermines its reliability.
Craig argues that a negative answer to the debate question needs support, distinguishes atheism from default agnosticism, and identifies his method as logic, evidence, and experience.
Absence of evidence supports God's nonexistence only if God's existence would probably produce more evidence than is observed, which Millican has not established.
This directly answers Millican's principal positive case for unbelief and invokes Craig's five affirmative arguments as the evidence already available.
Millican's contention that the apparent absence or weakness of evidence for God is itself evidence that God does not exist.
Craig distinguishes mere evidential absence from expected-but-missing evidence, applies that distinction to theism, and denies that a more evident world is highly probable given God.
The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin result supports an absolute cosmic beginning despite contracting models and does not depend on Einstein's gravitational equations.
The move defends the beginning premise of the cosmological argument against the principal scientific countermodels raised in Millican's opening speech.
Millican's appeal to prior contraction, quantum gravity, and the limited conclusion of the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem.
Craig supplies additional context about unstable contraction, stresses the theorem's generality, invokes Vilenkin's conclusion, and reiterates the need for a cause.
Something beginning without either a material or efficient cause is metaphysically impossible, and quantum-vacuum events do not provide counterexamples.
This defends the causal premise of the cosmological argument against experience-based, quantum-mechanical, and composition objections central to Millican's critique.
Millican's objections that ex nihilo causation is unobserved, quantum events may be uncaused, and the causal premise commits composition.
Craig distinguishes material from efficient causes, denies that a structured quantum vacuum is nothing, rejects the composition characterization, and locates cosmic potentiality in God.
A nonmaterial cause of the universe is best understood as an unembodied mind, while substance dualism makes immaterial personal causation coherent.
The move defends the personal-cause conclusion needed to connect a generic cause of the universe with the existence of a transcendent creator.
Millican's objection that there is no evidence for disembodied minds and no warrant for identifying a cosmic cause as personal.
Craig excludes material causes and causally inert abstract objects, argues that mental properties resist reduction, and analogizes divine action to a soul's bodily causation.
Naturalism cannot adequately ground intrinsic human value or binding moral obligations, whereas objective morality is more plausibly grounded in a divine lawgiver.
This supplies Craig's response to Millican's central challenge by identifying the claimed explanatory deficiency of atheistic accounts of moral value and duty.
Millican's claim that utilitarian, Kantian, and sentiment-based ethics can sustain belief-independent moral standards without God.
Craig argues that secular ethical systems presuppose unexplained human worth and that prescriptions require a prescriber, then presents God as morality's plausible foundation.
Fine-tuning offers at most a cautious design consideration and does not establish the morally perfect, omnipotent Christian God posited by Craig.
This is Millican's comprehensive answer to one of Craig's five affirmative arguments and challenges both its physical inference and specifically Christian conclusion.
Craig's argument that the universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is best explained by an intelligent designer identified with the Christian God.
Millican concedes intriguing coincidences but cites selection effects, unknown physics, multiverses, anti-God symmetry, cosmic inefficiency, inhospitable scale, and alien-incarnation implications.
Divine hiddenness does not establish atheism because further evidence might not bring more people into a saving relationship with God.
This directly contests the principal negative argument that a loving God would make his existence more evident to human beings.
Millican's claim that God's existence should be more obvious if such a God existed.
Craig distinguishes mere awareness of God's existence from salvific relationship and argues that additional disclosure might fail to improve the latter.
Both philosophical considerations about actual infinities and contemporary cosmology support a beginning of the universe, which therefore requires a cause.
The universe's beginning and need for a transcendent cause form a principal affirmative route from cosmological evidence to theism.
Millican's objections concerning infinity arithmetic, changing physics, the quantum vacuum, and causation.
Craig argues that divergent results from subtracting equal infinite collections are absurd in reality, cites current cosmology, and renews the causal premise.
The narrow life-permitting range and multiple independent instances of fine-tuning remain strong evidence for a cosmic designer despite Millican's objections.
Fine-tuning is one of the debate's principal evidential arguments for an intelligent creator and receives an extended defense against multiple objections.
Millican's objections about probability, unsettled physics, inefficiency, cosmic size, extraterrestrial life, and Christian doctrine.
Craig defends probability comparisons, invokes diverse fine-tuning evidence, rejects efficiency assumptions about God, and explains cosmic scale and possible extraterrestrial life.
Atheists can recognize and affirm intrinsic human worth and objective moral values without those values depending ontologically on God's existence.
This attacks the necessity premise of the moral argument by separating moral realism and moral knowledge from belief in a divine foundation.
Craig's claim that atheism provides no adequate foundation for objective morality or intrinsic human value.
Millican cites widespread non-theistic moral realism, questions the meaning of objectivity, and argues that rationality and other human characteristics can ground valuation.
The Gospel resurrection narratives provide weak evidence for God because they are late, dependent, partisan, discrepant, and unsupported by contemporary sources.
This directly contests the historical reliability and explanatory force of a principal affirmative argument for Christian theism rather than generic supernaturalism.
Craig's argument that accepted historical facts about Jesus are best explained by a divine resurrection.
Millican emphasizes Gospel authorship, source dependence, internal discrepancies, canonical selection, and extraordinary passion events absent from other contemporary records.
Without God, proposed foundations for objective moral value and obligation are arbitrary, whereas God can ground duties and enable moral knowledge.
The passage defends the affirmative moral argument's central grounding claim and answers both non-theistic moral realism and moral epistemology objections.
Millican's contention that non-theists can be moral realists, recognize values, and assign intrinsic human worth.
Craig questions why rational or sentient flourishing should be privileged, argues that obligations require a lawgiver, and distinguishes detecting values from grounding them.
The resurrection remains the best explanation of the accepted historical facts because skeptical rejection rests on prior naturalism rather than historical evidence.
This directly restores a principal Christian-theist argument after Millican's historical critique by defending both its factual basis and explanatory inference.
Millican's critique of Gospel discrepancies, dependence, late authorship, and lack of corroboration for extraordinary events.
Craig argues that cited skeptical historians accept burial, empty tomb, appearances, and belief formation, then attributes their rejection of resurrection to naturalism.
Religious experiences and resurrection reports require psychological and natural investigation, especially because comparable supernatural claims support incompatible traditions.
The move challenges two affirmative evidential pillars by proposing natural alternatives and arguing that similar support for incompatible supernatural beliefs undercuts them.
Craig's appeals to immediate religious experience and resurrection testimony as evidence for Christian theism.
Millican calls religious experience unreliable, urges experimental psychology, notes abundant miracle literature, and argues that naturally explicable and conflicting claims lack evidential force.
Intuition cannot establish that existence requires an efficient cause; only observation and scientific investigation can reveal causal principles applicable to the universe.
This attacks the causal premise and intuition-based methodology underlying the cosmological argument rather than merely disputing a peripheral factual claim.
Craig's defense of actual-infinity intuitions and the premise that things cannot begin without efficient causes.
Millican contrasts coherent mathematical treatment of zero and infinity with empirical causal inquiry, arguing that neither nothingness nor cosmic origins are observed cases.
The world's evil is empirical evidence against a perfectly good God, and limited supernatural evidence would not establish an omnipotent and omniscient deity.
The move supplies a direct evidential argument against the debated God and challenges the inference from isolated supernatural events to full classical theism.
Craig's skeptical-theist response to evil and his inference from resurrection and experience to the Christian God.
Millican argues that mysterious divine reasons can explain away any outcome, emphasizes goodness as a discriminating prediction, and denies that miracles establish classical divine attributes.
Greater uncertainty or lack of evidence does not enhance human freedom, because free choices ordinarily arise from reasons rather than arbitrary selection.
The move challenges a theistic explanation for divine hiddenness and an imperfect world by disputing the claimed relationship between evidential ambiguity and freedom.
The religious suggestion that limited evidence of God preserves or increases meaningful human freedom.
After the moderator raises a Christian free-will response to the problem of an imperfect world, Millican argues that reasons support rather than diminish genuinely free choice.
Evolution is theologically permissible, although mutation and natural selection may be scientifically insufficient to explain biological complexity within the available time.
The move answers a challenge about evolution by separating Christian theological commitments from a narrower scientific concern about evolutionary mechanisms.
Millican's contention that evolutionary history fits poorly with direct creation by an intelligent divine mind.
Craig accepts that evolutionary theory should be scientifically adjudicated while expressing doubt that the currently cited mechanisms fully explain the scale and speed of biological complexity.
Strict naturalized epistemology is self-undermining because its restriction of knowledge to logic and scientific evidence cannot itself be justified by those resources.
The move attacks the epistemic standard underlying Millican's objections and defends rational intuition as an additional source relevant to the debate's arguments.
Millican's repeated insistence that reliable knowledge in these matters must derive from experience rather than rational intuition.

Craig identifies a fundamental epistemological disagreement, arguing that empirically restricted methodology cannot establish its own exclusive authority and therefore cannot exclude rational intuition.
Empiricism is preferable to appeals to rational intuition because scientific experience repeatedly corrects intuitively compelling but mistaken conceptions of reality.
The move defends Millican's governing method for evaluating cosmological and other theistic arguments by grounding warranted belief in revisable experience.
Craig's charge that Millican's naturalized epistemology is self-defeating and improperly excludes rational intuition.
Millican denies dogmatic physicalism, emphasizes the evolving character of scientific categories, and uses relativity and quantum mechanics to illustrate experience overturning intuition.
Human cognitive limitations leave no secure basis for asserting that reality must have an ultimate cause, even if such a cause initially seems plausible.
The move directly resists the cosmological inference from a finite causal history to God by questioning whether evolved human cognition can settle ultimate reality.
The audience question and Craig's assertion that God is the ultimate cause required behind everything.
Millican concedes that an ultimate cause may sound plausible but argues that minds evolved for ordinary environments should not be presumed capable of resolving the universe's deepest structure.
Persistent unexplained fine-tuning could support a cosmic intelligence, but it would not warrant inferring an omnipotent or infinite God.
The move grants a conditional evidential case while sharply limiting its theological conclusion, directly calibrating what the fine-tuning argument could establish.
Craig's fine-tuning argument that the universe's life-permitting conditions support the existence of a transcendent designer.
Millican says fine-tuning might eventually demand explanation if future physics leaves the coincidences intact, yet regards that as evidence only for limited cosmic intelligence.
Natural evil may enable the greatest number of people freely to seek God, while most animals lack the higher-order awareness characteristic of human suffering.
The move supplies two substantive theodicies addressing natural evil: its possible role in salvation history and a proposed limitation on animal suffering.
The challenge that a loving God would not employ an evolutionary process involving extensive cruelty and animal pain.
Craig relates natural evil to God's purpose of freely bringing people into relationship with him, then argues that animals generally experience pain without reflective awareness of suffering.
A God who determines nature's rules could reveal himself clearly without suffering, and sincere rational inquiry can nevertheless end in justified unbelief.
The move combines the problem of evil with divine hiddenness, challenging both God's alleged need for suffering and the claim that sincere seekers find God.
Craig's claim that natural evil may maximize freely chosen salvation and forms part of God's intended framework.

Millican argues that an omnipotent rule-maker could make evidence rather than suffering conducive to relationship, then presents his own sincere theological study and resulting disbelief as a counterexample.
Jesus' exceptional influence is not itself proof, but the historical evidence for his resurrection supports accepting his claimed divine identity.
The move directly advances the Christian case identified in the motion by grounding Jesus' divine status in the alleged historical facts of the resurrection.
Craig acknowledges that historical influence alone does not establish truth, then redirects attention to gospel credibility, conceded historical facts, and the resurrection inference.
The resurrection evidence is weak because the gospels are late products of one community and religious psychology can sustain belief despite failed expectations.
The move directly contests the resurrection component of the Christian evidential case by offering historical-source and psychological alternatives to a miracle inference.
Craig's argument that the gospel resurrection facts and disciples' conduct support Jesus' resurrection and divine identity.
Millican questions the independence and timing of the gospel accounts and invokes research on intensified commitment after failed prophecy to challenge common assumptions about disciple sincerity.
